newsitem.title: USA: Digene reports progress on cancer test.
newsitem.headline: Digene reports progress on cancer test.

text.p: Digene Corp on Monday reported progress with a product that detects the presence of a primary cause of cervical cancer, the second most common cancer among women worldwide.
Digene's lead product, the Hybrid Capture HPV DNA test, detects the presence of HPV and is the only available HPV DNA test approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for in vitro diagnostic use.

Two presentations were reported at Papillomavirus Conference being held in Australia. The conference is a forum for new developments in the field of human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing and clinical research.
HPV is the primary cause of cervical cancer, which is the second most common cancer among women worldwide.

Preliminary results were announced from a clinical study being conducted with Kaiser Permanente and CYTYC Corp to show the effectiveness of using Digene's Hybrid Capture HPV DNA test for managing women with equivocal Pap smears in a managed care environment.

In the test, about 46,000 women, presenting for routine Pap smears, had cervical specimens collected for conventional cytology, liquid-based cytology (Cytyc's ThinPrep system), and HPV DNA detection by Digene's Hybrid Capture HPV DNA test.

Two types of equivocal Pap smears were studied -- ASCUS smears (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance), and AGUS smears (atypical glandular cells of undetermined significance). In preliminary results of the study, 81 percent of the equivocal Pap smears were classified on follow-up as being normal.

Under traditional protocols, all women with equivocal Pap smears are candidates for unnecessary, expensive and invasive follow-up procedures to resolve their status. In cases where such follow-up procedures are unavailable, these women are often referred for additional Pap smears.

The study revealed that by utilizing Digene's Hybrid Capture HPV DNA test to manage patients with equivocal Pap smears, 88 percent of women with high grade cervical disease (HSIL) were identified. In addition, the referral rate for colposcopy could be reduced to 38 percent, representing a 62 percent reduction versus established protocols. In the study, repeat Pap smears identified only 75 percent of HSIL. Digene expects to submit this new HPV detection technology to the FDA for pre-market approval in the spring of 1997.
